title: Digital Storage
subject: Introduction to ICT

topics.title: Hard Disks, RAID and NAS
topics.notes:
A hard disk drive, or HDD, retains data magnetically on rotating platters. Read/write heads access locations on the recording surfaces. It is non-volatile storage: saved data normally remains when power is removed. This differs from ordinary working RAM, which normally loses its contents without power. A drive is the physical device; a partition is a logical division of storage, and a file system organises files within a formatted volume.

Important characteristics include capacity, interface, access time, transfer performance, physical size, power requirements and suitability for the workload. RPM means revolutions per minute of the platters. Seek time involves positioning the heads; rotational delay involves waiting for the desired location to rotate into position. A higher RPM or larger cache alone does not establish the fastest drive for every workload. Small scattered requests and large continuous transfers place different demands on storage. The interface's advertised limit is not a guarantee of the drive's actual transfer rate.

An internal drive is installed inside a computer. An external HDD normally uses an enclosure and a connection such as USB; the enclosure may need separate power. Internal/external describes placement and connection, not a different recording principle. Handle HDDs carefully, especially during operation, and never open the sealed recording assembly for a classroom identification task.

RAID means redundant array of independent disks. RAID 0 stripes data without redundancy. RAID 1 mirrors copies across drives. RAID 5 combines striping with distributed parity and needs at least three drives; its ordinary single-parity design can tolerate one drive failure, not every kind of data loss. For two equal 1 TB drives, a simple RAID 1 mirror has about 1 TB usable capacity before formatting and other overhead. RAID is not a backup: deletion, malware or a common failure can affect the array's data.

Network-attached storage, or NAS, offers file access across a network. A NAS can use HDDs, SSDs and supported RAID arrangements, but NAS describes network file service, while RAID describes drive organisation. Shared folders need appropriate permissions and backups. Capacity labels also require care: 1 GB is 1,000,000,000 bytes, while 1 GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes. The same byte quantity has different decimal and binary numbers; file-system overhead can reduce usable space further.
examples: Two equal 1 TB drives in a simple RAID 1 mirror provide about 1 TB usable capacity before overhead.
A school NAS shares approved study files with authorised users over its network.
An external USB HDD still stores data magnetically, even though its connection differs from an internal drive.
mistakes: RAID 0 does not provide drive-failure redundancy.

Capacity, transfer rate and access latency are different measurements.

topics.title: Flash Storage and Solid-State Drives
topics.notes:
Flash memory is electrically rewritable non-volatile storage. Common examples include solid-state drives, memory cards and USB flash drives. Unlike an HDD, a typical flash SSD has no spinning platters or moving recording heads. It can access small scattered data with much lower mechanical delay, but actual performance depends on the device, controller, interface, workload, temperature and available resources. No single maximum speed describes every SSD or every transfer.

An SSD combines storage chips with a controller and supporting firmware. Flash has limited program/erase endurance, so controllers use techniques such as wear levelling and error correction. Wear levelling spreads writes rather than repeatedly concentrating them on a few cells. Endurance ratings describe specified conditions; they are not guarantees that data will remain readable forever. SSDs can fail, and important files still need verified backups. An SSD is not ordinary RAM merely because both use electronic components.

Form factor, interface and protocol are different. A 2.5-inch SSD can use SATA; an M.2 SSD can use SATA or PCIe with NVMe, depending on the model. M.2 describes a physical format rather than a promise that the device uses NVMe. Check the system's supported size, connector keying, interface and firmware requirements. A USB-C connector shape similarly does not guarantee one storage transfer speed. The slowest relevant part of the connection can limit a copy.

Memory cards include SD-family products used in cameras and other devices. Physical fit alone does not prove that the host supports every capacity family, file system or speed requirement. A passive microSD-to-SD adapter changes the physical presentation; it does not automatically make an incompatible host support every card. A USB flash drive combines flash storage with a USB interface and is useful for permitted file transfer. Use the operating system's supported removal procedure and wait for writes to finish before disconnecting removable storage.

The syllabus also names ExpressCard modules, a legacy notebook expansion format. Some modules provide flash-based storage or card-reading functions; others provide interfaces such as USB. ExpressCard is not a synonym for flash memory, and not every module stores files. Identify the actual function and model compatibility rather than treating every card-shaped device as a storage drive.
examples: An M.2 SATA SSD must be matched with a slot supporting its interface, not selected by shape alone.
A camera may require a supported SD capacity family and recording speed class.

topics.title: Optical Storage: CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray
topics.notes:
Optical storage uses a laser to read information from a disc. The drive detects differences in reflected light from the recording structure. A pressed read-only disc and a user-recordable disc do not necessarily form their marks by the same manufacturing process. The useful introductory distinction is optical reading rather than magnetic HDD recording or electronic flash storage.

CD, DVD and Blu-ray are different optical families with different supported formats and capacities. A common data CD is labelled 700 MB, a common single-layer DVD 4.7 GB, and a common single-layer Blu-ray Disc 25 GB. These are typical examples, not capacities of every disc. Dual-layer and other variants have different capacities; a common dual-layer Blu-ray is 50 GB. Actual available file space depends on the format and overhead. CD audio duration and data-file capacity are also different ways of describing use.

ROM indicates read-only media. An R designation commonly identifies recordable media intended for writing once rather than repeatedly erasing and rewriting the same recording areas. Some recordable sessions can be appended where the format and software allow it; write-once does not mean exactly one file. RW and BD-RE describe rewritable formats. Compatibility is specific: DVD-R and DVD+R are distinct formats, and a drive must support the intended disc family and write operation. A reader is not automatically a writer.

Blu-ray uses a shorter-wavelength blue-violet laser than the red laser used for DVD, helping support higher recording density in the format. A CD-only drive cannot read Blu-ray media. A Blu-ray drive may support earlier families, but read and write support should be checked in the exact model's specifications rather than assumed from the appearance of the tray.

Burning a disc means recording data with supported hardware and software. Merely copying a filename into a preparation window may not complete the write. Finish the recording as required, verify the contents and test the intended reading device. Handle discs by the edges or centre opening, protect their surfaces and store them appropriately. Scratches, heat, unsuitable storage and incompatible drives can make data inaccessible. Optical discs are not permanent guarantees of preservation; retain other copies and plan migration while compatible readers remain available.
examples: A 25 GB single-layer Blu-ray has a larger labelled capacity than a common 4.7 GB single-layer DVD.
A CD-R can hold several files, but it is not a repeatedly erasable CD-RW.
After writing a practice disc, reopen its files on a compatible reader to check the result.
mistakes: Typical capacity examples do not describe every layer count or variant.
A disc reader is not automatically a compatible disc writer.
A write-once disc is not limited to one file, and rewritable media do not promise infinite reuse.

topics.title: Magnetic Tape Storage
topics.notes:
Magnetic tape stores data as magnetic recordings on a long flexible strip contained in a reel or cartridge. A compatible tape drive reads and writes the medium. A tape cartridge and its drive are different objects, just as an optical disc differs from its reader. Tape is non-volatile and is used in managed backup and archive systems, including large collections of data.

Tape is fundamentally a sequential-access medium. Reaching a distant recording position requires physical movement along the tape. A tape index or catalogue can identify which file and location are needed, but it does not remove the mechanical positioning step. This differs from an HDD's direct block access or an SSD's electronic access. Tape can provide substantial sustained throughput when reading or writing long continuous streams, so sequential access does not mean that every tape operation has low transfer throughput.

Access latency and transfer rate must be distinguished. Latency includes preparation, mounting a cartridge if necessary, and positioning. Transfer rate describes how much data moves per unit time once streaming. A large restore can therefore have a preparation delay followed by efficient continuous reading. A workload that repeatedly requests scattered small files may be unsuitable even where an advertised streaming speed is high.

A tape library can automate cartridge storage and movement using robotic mechanisms. A catalogue tracks the files, media and required locations. Compatibility depends on the drive generation, cartridge format and supported read/write combinations; do not assume that every tape drive reads every old or new cartridge. If a product advertises compressed capacity, the actual benefit depends on the data. Already compressed video or encrypted data may not shrink as much as highly repetitive text.

Backup is a recoverable copy for restoration after loss or damage; an archive retains selected information for longer-term reference under a retention plan. A tape can serve either role according to how it is managed. Offline media can reduce exposure to online incidents when properly separated and controlled, but physical loss, unreadable media or missing encryption keys can still prevent recovery. Label cartridges, control access, follow storage guidance, keep compatible equipment available and test restores. Do not treat a successful copy log as a substitute for checking recoverability.

topics.title: Cloud Storage and Recoverable Copies
topics.notes:
Cloud storage keeps data on remotely managed storage systems accessed through a network service. The files still reside on physical hardware; cloud does not mean data exists without servers or storage media. A service can provide access through a website, application or API, and its permissions, retention features and limits depend on the service and account configuration.

Uploading transfers data to the service; downloading obtains a local copy. Synchronisation keeps selected locations aligned by propagating changes. A deletion in a synced folder can also be propagated to the service and other devices. Cloud backup can preserve recoverable versions according to a defined policy, but simple sync is not automatically an independent historical backup. Version history, recycle bins and retention can help recovery when supported and correctly configured; their availability and duration must be checked rather than assumed.

Cloud access depends on connectivity, account access and service availability. Some applications make selected files available offline by storing local copies. A placeholder or a filename visible in a folder does not prove that the full file is downloaded. Test the service's supported offline mode with a non-sensitive sample when access without a connection is required. Changes may need to synchronise when connectivity returns.

Use individual authorised accounts, strong authentication and suitable sharing permissions. Viewer and editor roles have different powers. A public link can expose information beyond the intended class; confirm recipients and access requirements. Encryption helps protect data under stated conditions, but it is not a substitute for sound permissions or recoverability. Shared responsibility means the provider operates parts of the service while the user or institution still manages account access, allowed data and appropriate configuration.

Plan storage by capacity, transfer needs, privacy, restore time and retention, not just the size of a free quota. Charges, quotas and features can change, so no specific free allocation or permanent price is promised here. Important work can use multiple copies with suitable separation, including an off-site copy; copies must be checked and protected. A restore test that opens the recovered file and compares its contents is more useful than merely seeing an upload icon. Do not delete original work until its retention and recovery requirements are satisfied.

A teacher shares a resource with named viewers rather than exposing it through an unrestricted public link.
An offline-ready file contains a local copy, while an online-only placeholder may need a connection.

short: Define digital storage and distinguish it from ordinary RAM.

Digital storage retains files and other data for later use. HDDs, flash drives and optical media normally retain saved data without power. Ordinary working RAM is normally volatile and holds current programs and data.
Name three HDD performance characteristics.

Access latency, sustained transfer rate and suitability for the request pattern matter. RPM describes platter rotation, but RPM alone does not prove overall performance. Capacity measures amount stored rather than access speed.
Distinguish an internal and an external HDD.

An internal drive is installed inside the computer; an external drive normally uses an enclosure and external connection. Both can use magnetic platters. The connection, enclosure and drive each affect practical use.
Compare RAID 0 and RAID 1.

RAID 0 stripes data without redundancy. RAID 1 mirrors data across drives. Two equal 1 TB drives in a simple mirror provide about 1 TB usable capacity before overhead. Neither arrangement replaces an independent recovery copy.
What is NAS and how does it differ from RAID?
NAS provides file access over a network. RAID organises multiple drives. A NAS can use a supported RAID arrangement, but network file service and drive organisation are separate concepts.
Why is M.2 not a synonym for NVMe?
M.2 is a physical form factor. M.2 SSDs can use SATA or PCIe/NVMe according to the device and host support. Compatibility needs more than a similar connector shape.
What are wear levelling and one SSD limitation?
Wear levelling distributes writes across flash locations. Flash has finite program/erase endurance and an SSD can fail, so wear management does not remove the need for backups.
Distinguish recordable and rewritable optical media.

Recordable R media are intended for write-once recording areas, while RW or BD-RE media support rewriting. A recordable disc can hold multiple files; the drive must support the format and intended write operation.
Explain sequential access in tape storage.

Tape must move physically along the medium to reach a recording position. An index can identify a location but does not remove positioning. Streaming throughput after positioning differs from the initial access delay.
Distinguish native and compressed tape capacity.

Native capacity is specified without relying on compression savings. Compressed capacity assumes compressible data. Already compressed or encrypted input may obtain little additional reduction, so the larger number is not guaranteed for every dataset.
How do cloud sync and backup differ?

Sync propagates changes between selected locations, potentially including deletions. A backup preserves recoverable data under a retention policy. Sync, version history and an independent backup must be evaluated by actual recovery behaviour.
How can a backup be checked?

Restore a permitted sample to a separate location, open it and compare its contents with the source. Also confirm that required media, credentials, software and encryption keys remain available. A successful copy log alone is incomplete evidence.
long: Explain HDD operation, characteristics and internal/external use.
Recording
Data is represented magnetically on rotating platters and accessed by read/write heads. Saved data normally remains without power. Do not confuse a physical drive with its partitions or file system.
Performance

Head positioning and rotational delay contribute to access latency. Transfer rate measures data moved over time. RPM, interface limits and cache are relevant but do not alone establish performance for every workload.
Placement

Internal drives are installed within the system. An external enclosure provides an external connection and may require its own power. The enclosure does not turn the recording medium into flash or optical storage.
Capacity and care

Use clear units: 1 GB is 1,000,000,000 bytes and 1 GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes. Overhead affects usable space. Handle drives according to the manual, keep independent recovery copies and leave the sealed recording assembly unopened.
Compare RAID, NAS and an independent backup for a school.
Drive organisation
RAID 0 stripes without redundancy. RAID 1 mirrors. RAID 5 uses distributed parity and needs at least three drives. These examples address selected drive-level behaviour, not every cause of data loss.
Network service
A NAS provides shared file access over a network. It can contain supported HDDs or SSDs and may use RAID. Folder permissions determine who can read or change resources.
Recovery copy

A separate backup retains recoverable work according to a plan. Live deletion or corruption can affect an array and can also propagate through sync, so availability mechanisms must not be confused with historical recovery.
School example

Place approved class files in a permission-controlled shared folder, maintain separate recoverable copies and test restoration. Verify which failure each measure addresses instead of assuming the presence of RAID guarantees every file is safe.
Describe flash devices and the compatibility checks needed before use.
Technology

Flash is electrically rewritable and non-volatile. A typical SSD uses chips and a controller without spinning platters. Wear levelling and error correction support management, but endurance and reliability remain limited.
SSD formats
2.5-inch and M.2 describe physical formats. SATA, PCIe and NVMe describe different interface or access aspects. Check the exact host and drive specifications rather than equating M.2 with NVMe.
Cards and USB

SD-family cards must match host support for their family, capacity and required performance. USB drive speed depends on the device and connection path. A passive card adapter changes physical presentation rather than adding every missing capability.
Legacy expansion and handling

ExpressCard is a legacy notebook expansion format with storage-related and other modules. Identify the function first. Finish writes and use supported removal procedures for removable media; keep verified recovery copies.
Compare CD, DVD and Blu-ray and explain a checked recording workflow.
Optical reading
A compatible drive uses a laser to detect recorded optical information. Blu-ray uses blue-violet light with an optical design supporting denser recording than DVD.
Typical capacities
Common labelled examples are a 700 MB data CD, a 4.7 GB single-layer DVD and a 25 GB single-layer Blu-ray. Layers and variants change capacity; these examples do not describe every disc.
Recording types

ROM is read-only. R media are write-once recordable; RW or BD-RE support rewriting. Several files can be stored on a recordable disc. Reading a format and writing it require separately supported capabilities.
Workflow

Choose suitable media and a compatible writer, select non-sensitive practice files, complete recording with supported software and verify the finished files on the intended reader. Protect surfaces and retain other copies; no disc is a guarantee of permanent preservation.
Explain magnetic tape performance and its backup/archive role.
Medium and access
A drive reads a magnetic flexible strip in a cartridge. Physical sequential positioning is needed even where an index identifies a file location. A compatible cartridge and drive must be available.
Performance
Mounting and positioning can delay first access; sustained streaming rate measures transfer after positioning. Large continuous workloads and scattered small-file requests have different demands.
Capacity and purpose

Native capacity does not depend on compression savings. Compressed capacity depends on input characteristics. Backups support recovery; archives retain selected information under a longer-term reference plan.
Recoverability

Track media and locations, protect required keys, follow handling guidance and test restores. A properly separated offline cartridge can reduce exposure to online incidents, but loss, damage, incompatibility or unavailable keys can still prevent recovery.
Design a recoverable storage workflow for a student project.
Working copy
Save current work in an approved local location and use meaningful filenames. Ordinary unsaved RAM contents are not a retained project copy. Match available storage and performance to the task.
Additional copies

Maintain suitable separate copies, including a copy away from the same physical location where appropriate. A mirror or live sync alone does not preserve every earlier state. Specify what is retained and for how long.
Cloud use

Use an authorised account and suitable viewer/editor permissions. Check upload completion, offline-file availability when needed and the actual version/retention policy. The service uses physical infrastructure and still needs customer-side access management.
Restore test

Recover a non-sensitive sample to a separate location, open it and compare contents. Record the media, software, account and keys needed for recovery. Preserve the original until the required copies and recovery checks are complete.
practical: On a permitted device, observe storage information in system settings. Record each visible device or volume, its reported capacity and unit, and whether the technology is known from the model documentation. Do not initialise, format, partition or open a drive.

On paper, compare 1 GB with 1 GiB. Then calculate the usable unique-data capacity before overhead for two equal 1 TB drives in a simple RAID 1 mirror. Explain why this is not an independent backup.
Correct byte multipliers and about 1 TB mirrored usable capacity, with a recovery limitation.
Copy and reopen a practice file

Create a non-sensitive sample in an approved practice folder. Copy it to a second permitted storage location, wait for completion and open the copy. Compare text and file size; use supported removal for removable media. Retain the original.
A readable matching copy and a record of source/destination; two folders on one drive are not claimed to protect against failure of that drive.

Using labels, photographs or manuals, identify CD/DVD/Blu-ray families, ROM/R/RW/RE markings where relevant, and a tape cartridge with its required drive. State typical versus model-specific capacity and native versus compressed tape capacity.
A comparison that does not assume every drive reads or writes every medium; no equipment disassembly is required.

Draw a project storage plan with working copy, separate recoverable copy and an appropriately separated location. If an approved account is already available, upload only a non-sensitive sample, download it separately and compare contents. Otherwise complete the same recovery demonstration between permitted local locations and explain the cloud steps on paper. Do not change subscriptions or expose private files.
A checked restored sample, named dependencies and suitable sharing/retention choices; sync alone is not presented as a complete backup.

diagramDescription: The working project is saved on local storage. A separate recovery copy is made to another permitted device. An off-site copy adds location separation, for example through an appropriately managed cloud service. The arrows represent checked copying, not automatic sync or RAID. Real recovery requires readable contents and the necessary access, software and keys.

| NAS | Network file access | A particular RAID level |
| Sync | Propagating selected changes | Protection from propagated deletion |
